'''''Eucalyptus dalrympleana''''', commonly known as '''mountain gum''', '''mountain white gum''', '''white gum''' and '''broad-leaved ribbon gum''',<ref name="CANBR">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' |url=https://apps.lucidcentral.org/euclid/text/entities/eucalyptus_dalrympleana_subsp._dalrympleana.htm |publisher=Euclid: Centre for Australian National Biodiversity Research |access-date=4 June 2020}}</ref> is a species of tree that is [[Endemism|endemic]] to southeastern Australia. It has smooth bark, lance-shaped adult leaves, flower buds in groups of three or seven, white flowers and cup-shaped, bell-shaped or hemispherical fruit.[[File:Myrtales - Eucalyptus dalrympleana 12.jpg|thumb|Flower buds]][[File:Myrtales - Eucalyptus dalrympleana 13.jpg|thumb|Immature fruit]]

==Description==
''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' is a tree that typically grows to a height of {{cvt|40|m}} and forms a [[lignotuber]]. It has smooth white to yellowish bark, sometimes with a short stocking of rough bark. Young plants and [[coppice]] regrowth have leaves arranged in opposite pairs and are egg-shaped or heart-shaped to more or less round, {{cvt|25-70|mm}} long and wide. Adult leaves are arranged alternately, lance-shaped to curved, the same colour on both sides, {{cvt|80-220|mm}} long and {{cvt|10-40|mm}} wide on a [[Petiole (botany)|petiole]] {{cvt|12-35|mm}} long. The flower buds are arranged in groups of three or seven in leaf [[wikt:axil|axil]]s on a [[Peduncle (botany)|peduncle]] {{cvt|3-12|mm}} long, the individual buds [[Sessility (botany)|sessile]] or on a [[Pedicel (botany)|pedicel]] up to {{cvt|3|mm}} long. Mature buds are oval, green to yellow, {{cvt|6-10|mm}} long and {{cvt|3-6|mm}} wide with a conical to rounded [[Operculum (botany)|operculum]]. Flowering mainly occurs between March and June and the flowers are white. The fruit is a woody cup-shaped, bell-shaped or hemispherical [[Capsule (botany)|capsule]] {{cvt|3-8|mm}} long and {{cvt|5-9|mm}} wide.<ref name="CANBR" /><ref name="RBGV">{{cite web |last1=Brooker |first1=M. Ian |last2=Slee |first2=Andrew V. |title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' |url=https://vicflora.rbg.vic.gov.au/flora/taxon/b1be1c09-c69b-4e2d-8d10-2aa76bae121e |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria |access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="RBGS">{{cite web |last1=Hill |first1=Ken |title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' |url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/NSWfl.pl?page=nswfl&lvl=sp&name=Eucalyptus~dalrympleana |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden Sydney |access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="ABRS">{{cite web |last1=Chippendale |first1=George M. |title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' |url=https://profiles.ala.org.au/opus/foa/profile/Eucalyptus%20dalrympleana |publisher=Australian Biological Resources Study, Department of the Environment and Energy, Canberra |access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref>

==Taxonomy and naming==
''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' was first [[Species description|formally described]] in 1920 by [[Joseph Maiden]] from a specimen collected by [[Wilfred Alexander Watt de Beuzeville|Wilfred de Beuzeville]] near [[Yarrangobilly, New South Wales|Yarrangobilly]]. The description was published in Maiden's book, ''The Forest Flora of New South Wales''.<ref name=APNI>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana''|url= https://id.biodiversity.org.au/instance/apni/454919|publisher=APNI|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref><ref name="ANBG">{{cite web |title=Beuzeville, Wilfred Alexander Watt de (1884 - 1954) |url=http://www.anbg.gov.au/biography/beuzeville-wilfred.html |publisher=Australian National Herbarium |access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> The [[Botanical name|specific epithet]] (''dalrympleana'') honours the forester, Richard Dalrymple Hay.<ref name="CANBR" />

In 1962, [[Lawrence Alexander Sidney Johnson|Lawrie Johnson]] described two subspecies and the names have been accepted by the [[Australian Plant Census]]:
* ''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' <small> Maiden</small> subsp. ''dalrympleana''<ref name=APC1>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' subsp. ''dalrympleana''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/69821|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> has flower buds arranged in groups of three;<ref name="RBGS" />
* ''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' subsp. ''heptantha'' <small> L.A.S.Johnson</small><ref name=APC2>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' subsp. ''heptantha''|url= https://biodiversity.org.au/nsl/services/apc-format/display/69839|publisher=Australian Plant Census|access-date=21 May 2019}}</ref> has flower buds and flowers in groups of seven.<ref name="RBGS" />

==Distribution and habitat==
Mountain gum grows in woodland and forest at higher elevations in far south-eastern [[Queensland]], [[New South Wales]], [[Victoria (Australia)|Victoria]], [[South Australia]] and [[Tasmania]]. Subspecies ''heptantha'' is only found in far south-eastern Queensland and on the [[Northern Tablelands|northern tablelands]] of New South Wales. Subspecies ''dalrympleana'' occurs south from the [[Central Tablelands|central]] and [[Southern Tablelands|southern]] tablelands of New South Wales.<ref name="RBGV" /><ref name="RBGS" /> The species is rare in South Australia where it only occurs in the [[Mount Lofty Ranges]].<ref name="SSA">{{cite web |title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' ssp. ''dalrympleana'' (Myrtaceae) Mountain White Gum |url=https://spapps.environment.sa.gov.au/SeedsOfSA/speciesinformation.html?rid=1811 |publisher=Seeds of South Australia |access-date=22 May 2019}}</ref>

==Use in horticulture==
In cultivation in the [[UK]], ''E. dalrympleana'' is fully hardy down to {{convert|-15 |C|F|abbr=on}} but prefers some shelter. It grows best in full sun. It has gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web|title=''Eucalyptus dalrympleana'' AGM|url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/32644/Eucalyptus-dalrympleana/Details |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society|access-date=19 June 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 36 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | access-date = 18 February 2018}}</ref>
